title: How stationary waves form

prerequisites.boundary_note: The verified Lesson 1 handoff supplies superposition and point-by-point signed addition. Topic 7 is an external prerequisite supplying progressive-wave and phase language.

prior_knowledge_summary: Students can apply superposition at the same place and time, construct a resultant point by point, and read phase and displacement on progressive-wave graphs.
new_learning: Formation of a stationary wave by two same-type waves of equal frequency and equal amplitude travelling in opposite directions and overlapping.
Fixed node and antinode positions explained by repeated superposition.
not_yet_taught: experimental arrangements for strings, air columns or microwaves

evidence_basis.p1_mapping_note: No P1 lesson assignments inferred because canonical P1 mapping remains at module grain.

visual_rules.style: colourful hand-drawn teacher sketch on rectangular white paper

blocks.title: A wave pattern that refuses to travel
content: A hand sends waves along a rope towards a wall. The individual waves travel, yet a repeating pattern can appear to stay in one place. How can moving waves make a stationary pattern?
The wall sends a reflected wave back through the incoming wave. The answer must come from what happens during their continuous overlap.

figure.purpose: Pose the contradiction between moving component waves and a stationary resultant pattern.
figure.brief: Three-frame teacher sketch on white paper: pulse train travelling right, reflection at wall, fixed-looking loop pattern. Sparse arrows, no node labels yet.
figure.alt_text: Incoming and reflected waves overlap to produce a pattern that appears fixed.

blocks.title: What the two waves must share
content: For the overlap pattern to repeat in fixed places, the two waves must stay matched. They are the same type, have equal frequency and equal amplitude, and travel through the same medium in opposite directions.
In the same medium, equal frequency means the waves also have equal wavelength and speed. Their directions differ, but their timing pattern matches.

figure.purpose: Compare the required properties of the two component waves.
figure.brief: Hand-drawn comparison table for wave A and wave B: same type, equal frequency, equal amplitude, equal wavelength, equal speed, opposite directions. Use arrows to emphasise direction.
figure.alt_text: Two matched waves have equal frequency and amplitude but travel oppositely.

blocks.title: Superposition repeats the pattern
content: At every point, the instantaneous resultant is the algebraic sum of the two component displacements. This is the Lesson 1 rule applied continuously.
Half a period later, both component waves have changed displacement. Adding them again gives the inverted shape of the same fixed pattern. Another half period returns the original shape.
The resultant pattern does not transfer its shape along the medium. Its special positions stay fixed.

figure.purpose: Show graphical stationary-wave formation across time.
figure.brief: Four aligned time snapshots at 0, T/4, T/2 and 3T/4. Show two thin coloured component waves and a bold resultant. Keep horizontal positions aligned and fixed.
figure.alt_text: Four snapshots show opposite travelling waves adding to a fixed stationary-wave pattern.

blocks.title: Nodes stay still

definition.displayed_content: a point or position on a stationary wave with zero amplitude

content: At certain fixed positions, the two component displacements are always equal and opposite. Their sum is always zero, so that part of the medium never moves from equilibrium.
Zero amplitude means zero maximum displacement over the entire oscillation, not merely zero displacement at one instant.

figure.purpose: Distinguish a permanent zero-amplitude node from an ordinary equilibrium crossing.
figure.brief: Overlay three stationary-wave snapshots. Mark fixed intersections common to all snapshots as nodes. Contrast with one unmarked point that crosses equilibrium but later moves.
figure.alt_text: Several snapshots share fixed zero-amplitude node positions.

blocks.title: Antinodes move most

definition.displayed_content: a position in a stationary wave where the oscillation amplitude is maximum

content: Halfway through each loop, the component waves repeatedly reinforce most strongly. The resultant displacement changes direction with time, but the amplitude there is larger than at neighbouring points.
An antinode is a fixed position of maximum amplitude. It is not a crest that travels along the medium.

figure.purpose: Locate maximum-amplitude positions and separate antinodes from travelling crests.
figure.brief: Two opposite extreme stationary-wave shapes with nodes fixed and antinodes marked at loop centres. Use vertical double arrows at antinodes.
figure.alt_text: Antinodes at loop centres reach maximum displacement in opposite directions.

blocks.title: Read a pair of snapshots
content: Imagine two equal waves at one instant. At position P their displacements are +2 mm and -2 mm, so the resultant is 0 mm. A quarter period later they are again equal and opposite at P. P is evidence for a node.
At position Q the displacements are +2 mm and +2 mm, giving +4 mm. Half a period later both are -2 mm, giving -4 mm. Q oscillates through the largest range and is an antinode.
The check uses time: a node remains zero in every snapshot, while an antinode changes instantaneous displacement but keeps maximum amplitude.

figure.purpose: Model how multiple snapshots identify nodes and antinodes.
figure.brief: Annotated two-position table for P and Q at two times, showing component signed displacements and resultants. Colour inputs and resultants consistently.
figure.alt_text: Signed component displacements identify P as a node and Q as an antinode.

blocks.title: Formation in one causal chain
content: A source sends a wave towards a boundary. Reflection supplies a same-type wave of equal frequency and equal amplitude travelling in the opposite direction. The two waves overlap and superpose.
Repeated point-by-point addition creates fixed positions of zero amplitude and fixed positions of maximum amplitude. These are nodes and antinodes, so the resultant is a stationary wave.
Do not use one frozen picture alone to identify zero amplitude. Compare the pattern through time.

figure.purpose: Summarise the complete causal chain without experimental detail reserved for Lesson 4.
figure.brief: Flow diagram: incident wave, reflection, opposite matched waves, superposition, fixed nodes and antinodes, stationary wave. Rectangular white-paper sketch.
figure.alt_text: A causal flow from reflection and overlap to fixed nodes and antinodes.

concepts_taught: stationary-wave formation by oppositely travelling same-type waves of equal frequency and equal amplitude
fixed nodes and antinodes from repeated superposition
misconceptions_addressed: A stationary wave is made from waves that do not travel.
Any point at equilibrium in one snapshot is a node.
An antinode is a crest travelling along the medium.
skills_students_can_now_use: Identify nodes and antinodes across snapshots.
Use superposition to justify fixed zero and maximum amplitude positions.
next_lesson_can_assume: Stationary waves form from matched waves travelling oppositely and overlapping.
Nodes and antinodes occupy fixed positions.
